# Trochoid

*Image: Cycloid f.gif.* A [cycloid](wikipedia://en/41638) (a common trochoid) generated by a rolling circle

::: {#o1 .subject cue=lead name="Trochoid"}

In [geometry](wikipedia://en/18973446), a **trochoid** (el) is a [roulette](wikipedia://en/846500) curve formed by a [circle](wikipedia://en/6220) rolling along a [line](wikipedia://en/946975). It is the [curve](wikipedia://en/89246) traced out by a point fixed to a circle (where the point may be on, inside, or outside the circle) as it rolls along a straight line. If the point is on the circle, the trochoid is called *common* (also known as a [cycloid](wikipedia://en/41638)); if the point is inside the circle, the trochoid is *curtate*; and if the point is outside the circle, the trochoid is *prolate*. The word "trochoid" was coined by [Gilles de Roberval](wikipedia://en/196880), referring to the special case of a cycloid.[^o3]

:::

## Basic description {#Basic_description}

*Image: TrohoidH1,25.gif.* A prolate trochoid with $b/a = 5/4$

*Image: TrohoidH0,8.gif.* A curtate trochoid with $b/a = 4/5$

As a circle of radius $a$ rolls without slipping along a line $L$, the center $C$ moves parallel to $L$, and every other point $P$ in the rotating plane rigidly attached to the circle traces the curve called the trochoid. Let $\overline{CP} = b$. [Parametric equations](wikipedia://en/576108) of the trochoid for which $L$ is the $x$-axis are

$$\begin{aligned} x &= a\theta - b \sin \theta \\ y &= a - b \cos \theta \end{aligned}$$

where $\theta$ is the variable angle through which the circle rolls.[^o5]

### Curtate, common, prolate {#Curtate,_common,_prolate}

If $P$ lies inside the circle ($b < a$), on its circumference ($b = a$), or outside ($b > a$), the trochoid is described as being curtate ("contracted"), common, or prolate ("extended"), respectively.[^o7] A curtate trochoid is traced by a pedal (relative to the ground) when a normally geared bicycle is pedaled along a straight line.[^o8] A [prolate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prolate) trochoid is traced by the tip of a paddle (relative to the water's surface) when a boat is driven with constant velocity by paddle wheels; this curve contains loops. A common trochoid, also called a [cycloid](wikipedia://en/41638), has [cusps](wikipedia://en/6851758) at the points where $P$ touches the line $L$.

## General description {#General_description}

A more general approach would define a trochoid as the [locus](wikipedia://en/542465) of a point $(x,y)$ [orbiting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit) at a constant rate around an axis located at $(x',y')$,

$$x=x'+r_1\cos(\omega_1 t+\phi_1),\ y=y'+r_1\sin(\omega_1 t+\phi_1),\ r_1>0,$$

which axis is being translated in the *x-y*-plane at a constant rate in *either* a straight line,

$$\begin{array}{lcl} x'=x_0+v_{2x} t,\ y'=y_0+v_{2y} t\\ \therefore x = x_0+r_1\cos(\omega_1 t+\phi_1)+v_{2x} t,\ y = y_0+r_1 \sin(\omega_1 t+\phi_1)+v_{2y} t,\\ \end{array}$$

or a circular path (another orbit) around $(x_0,y_0)$ (the [hypotrochoid](wikipedia://en/1547158)/[epitrochoid](wikipedia://en/1547292) case),

$$\begin{array}{lcl} x' = x_0+r_2\cos(\omega_2 t+\phi_2),\ y' = y_0+r_2\sin(\omega_2 t+\phi_2),\ r_2\ge 0\\ \therefore x = x_0+r_1\cos(\omega_1 t+\phi_1)+r_2\cos(\omega_2 t+\phi_2),\ y = y_0+r_1 \sin(\omega_1 t+\phi_1)+r_2\sin(\omega_2 t+\phi_2),\\ \end{array}$$

The ratio of the rates of motion and whether the moving axis translates in a straight or circular path determines the shape of the trochoid. In the case of a straight path, one full rotation coincides with one period of a [periodic](wikipedia://en/76848) (repeating) locus. In the case of a circular path for the moving axis, the locus is periodic only if the ratio of these angular motions, $\omega_1/\omega_2$, is a rational number, say $p/q$, where $p$ & $q$ are [coprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coprime), in which case, one period consists of $p$ orbits around the moving axis and $q$ orbits of the moving axis around the point $(x_0,y_0)$. The special cases of the [epicycloid](wikipedia://en/713354) and [hypocycloid](wikipedia://en/592735), generated by tracing the locus of a point on the perimeter of a circle of radius $r_1$ while it is rolled on the perimeter of a stationary circle of radius $R$, have the following properties:

$$\begin{array}{lcl} \text{epicycloid: }&\omega_1/\omega_2&=p/q=r_2/r_1=R/r_1+1,\ |p-q| \text{ cusps}\\ \text{hypocycloid: }&\omega_1/\omega_2&=p/q=-r_2/r_1=-(R/r_1-1),\ |p-q|=|p|+|q| \text{ cusps} \end{array}$$

where $r_2$ is the radius of the orbit of the moving axis. The number of cusps given above also hold true for any epitrochoid and hypotrochoid, with "cusps" replaced by either "radial maxima" or "radial minima".
